title: Bonds & Interest Rates
description: Coupons, prices, and why a bond is a loan with a date on it.
wolfLine: The price moves. The maturity date is the plan.

coupon.definition: The interest a bond pays you. A $40 coupon is $40 a year, usually split into smaller payments.
coupon.example: A $1,000 bond with a $40 coupon pays $40 a year.

maturity.definition: The date a bond ends. If the issuer pays, you get the face value back then.
maturity.example: A bond that matures in 10 years pays the $1,000 face value in year 10.

yield.definition: What a bond pays you compared with the price you paid, as a percent. Coupon divided by price.
yield.example: A $40 coupon on a bond you buy for $800 is a 5% yield.

lessons.title: How a Bond Works
lessons.summary: You lend. They pay interest. Then they pay you back.

steps.title: The loan, written down
steps.body: A [[bond]] has a face value, a [[coupon]], and a [[maturity]]. The coupon is the interest. Maturity is the end date. This page is a simple Treasury: you lend $1,000, it pays $40 a year, and it ends in 10 years.

doc.title: A Treasury bond
doc.subtitle: You are the lender
doc.note: If you hold to maturity and the issuer pays, the face value comes back. The coupon is the interest along the way.

steps.prompt: How many dollars is the coupon each year?
steps.explain: The coupon is $40 a year on the $1,000 face value.

doc.title: A Treasury bond
doc.subtitle: You are the lender
doc.note: If you hold to maturity and the issuer pays, the face value comes back. The coupon is the interest along the way.

steps.prompt: If you buy this bond for the $1,000 face value, what is the yield in percent?
If you hold this bond to maturity and the issuer pays, you get the $1,000 face value back.
steps.explain: The coupons were the interest. Maturity returns the face value. Selling early is a different price.

steps.prompt: Who is the lender on this page?
choices: The government is lending to you
You are lending to the government
The bond is a share of a company
steps.explain: A bond is a loan you make. A stock would be ownership.

lessons.title: Treasuries and Corporate Bonds
lessons.summary: Same shape of loan, different borrower.

steps.title: Who borrowed
steps.body: A Treasury is a [[bond]] from the US government. A corporate bond is a loan to a company. The company can fail to pay. The higher [[coupon]] on a corporate bond is pay for that extra chance. Neither one is a stock.

steps.prompt: Which borrower can more realistically fail to pay you back?
choices: The US government, on a Treasury
A company, on a corporate bond
steps.explain: A company can run out of money. That extra chance is why corporate bonds usually offer more interest.

steps.prompt: A Treasury bond’s price can fall before maturity.
steps.explain: You can sell early for less than face value. Holding to maturity is what brings the face value back, if the issuer pays.

steps.prompt: Why might a corporate bond pay a higher coupon than a Treasury?
choices: Because the company is the government
Because lenders want pay for the chance the company cannot pay
steps.explain: More chance of a missed payment, more interest. It is not free extra money.

steps.prompt: A bond from the US government is called a ___.
steps.explain: Treasury. A corporate bond is the loan to a company.

lessons.title: When Rates Rise
lessons.summary: Old bonds get cheaper so they can compete.

steps.title: The seesaw
steps.body: You hold a bond with a $40 [[coupon]]. New bonds start paying more, because rates rose. Nobody wants your $40 if they can get more on a new bond, unless your bond’s price falls. A lower price raises the [[yield]] for the buyer.

steps.prompt: Your $40 coupon bond falls to a price of $800. What is the buyer’s yield, in percent?
The face value is $1,000 and the price is $800. How many dollars below face is that price?
steps.explain: $1,000 − $800 = $200. That gap is the price risk if you sell now.

steps.prompt: When interest rates rise, the price of an existing bond generally falls.
steps.explain: The old coupon has to compete. The price does the competing.

steps.prompt: You do not need the money until maturity, and the issuer is paying. What does the $800 price mean for you?
choices: You already lost the $200 for good
It is the price if you sell today. Maturity can still pay the $1,000 face value
steps.explain: The coupon is still $40. The $800 matters if you sell. Maturity, if the issuer pays, is the face value.

lessons.title: CDs and I Bonds
lessons.summary: Two ways to lock money, with rules.

steps.title: Read the lock
steps.body:
A CD is a bank deposit for a set term. CDs at a bank are FDIC insured, generally up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Cashing out early usually costs a penalty.

An I bond is a US savings bond. The rate mixes a fixed part with inflation and changes in May and November, so this course will not grade today’s rate. Electronic I bonds are capped at $10,000 per person per calendar year. You cannot cash one in the first 12 months. Cash out before 5 years and you lose the last 3 months of interest.

steps.prompt: What is the electronic I bond purchase cap, in dollars, for one person in one calendar year?
steps.explain: TreasuryDirect caps electronic I bonds at $10,000 per person per calendar year. The rate itself changes twice a year.

steps.prompt: You can cash a brand-new I bond after one month.
steps.explain: The first 12 months are locked. Before 5 years, leaving also costs the last 3 months of interest.

steps.prompt: You cash an I bond in year 3. What do the rules take?
steps.explain: Past 12 months you can cash out. Before 5 years you forfeit the last 3 months of interest.

steps.prompt: A CD and an I bond are the same product.
steps.explain: A CD is a bank deposit. An I bond is a savings bond from the US Treasury, with its own cap and lockup.

lessons.title: Yield
lessons.summary: The coupon only tells the story at the price you paid.

steps.title: Price changes the percent
steps.body: [[Yield]] is the [[coupon]] divided by the price you pay. A $30 coupon on a $1,000 price is 3%. The same $30 on a lower price is a higher yield. This is the current yield, a beginner version.

steps.prompt: A bond pays a $30 coupon and you buy it for $1,000. What is the yield, in percent?
The same $30 coupon is on a bond priced at $600. What is the yield, in percent?
The coupon stays $30 and the price falls. What happens to the yield?
steps.explain: Yield is coupon ÷ price. A smaller price makes a bigger percent.

steps.prompt: Yield and coupon are always the same number.
steps.explain: They match when you pay face value. Pay a different price and the yield moves.

lessons.title: Bonds in a Portfolio
lessons.summary: The steadier slice, not a zero-risk slice.

steps.title: Why they sit next to stocks
steps.body: [[Stock]]s usually swing more. [[Bond]]s often swing less, and they often move differently. That is why a [[portfolio]] uses both. Bonds can still lose money if you sell when rates have risen, or if a company cannot pay.

steps.prompt: What job do bonds usually have next to stocks?
choices: To be a steadier slice that often moves differently
steps.explain: Steadier, not frozen. The emergency fund is still cash.

steps.prompt: A bond fund cannot lose money in a year when rates rise.
steps.explain: Rising rates push existing bond prices down. A fund that holds those bonds can fall.

steps.prompt: You need the money in one year. A 10-year bond is a weak fit because…
choices: You might have to sell before maturity, at a lower price
steps.explain: A short timeline wants cash. A long bond’s price can be down in the exact year you sell.

steps.prompt: A portfolio is $8,000 in stocks and $2,000 in bonds. How many dollars are in the bond slice?
steps.explain: The bond slice is the $2,000. The mix itself is the next unit’s subject.

lessons.title: A CD or a Treasury
lessons.summary: Same dollars in this example. Different borrower.

steps.title: Line them up
steps.body: Both pages pay $40 on $1,000, so 4%. The CD is a bank deposit. The Treasury is a loan to the US government. The example uses the same rate on purpose, so the choice is about the borrower and the rules, not about chasing a higher number.

docs.title: One-year CD at a bank
docs.subtitle: FDIC insured, generally up to $250,000 at that bank
docs.note: Leaving early usually costs a penalty.

docs.title: One-year Treasury
docs.subtitle: A loan to the US government
docs.note: Hold it the year and, if the issuer pays, the $1,000 comes back.

steps.prompt: Which page is a loan to the US government?
steps.explain: The Treasury is the government loan. The CD is the bank deposit, with FDIC insurance up to the usual limit.

steps.prompt: How many dollars of interest does each page pay in this example?
steps.explain: Both are $1,000 × 0.04 = $40. The rate match is the point of the comparison.

steps.prompt: You might need the cash in three months. Which fits better than either locked page?
choices: A savings account you can take money from
steps.explain: Both locked pages want the year. Three months wants the savings account.

steps.prompt: Because both pay $40, they are the same product.
steps.explain: The dollars match. The borrower, the insurance, and the early-exit rules do not.

lessons.title: Helen Holds
lessons.summary: The price on the screen is not the maturity check.

story.title: The screen says $800
story.body:
Helen owns a **$1,000** Treasury with a **$40** coupon. It matures in **10 years**, and she does not need the money until then.

Rates rise. If she sold today she would get **$800**. The coupon is still $40.

steps.title: Meet Helen
steps.body:
Helen is 36 and a school librarian. She owns the $1,000 Treasury from this unit: a $40 coupon, maturity in 10 years. She does not need the money until then.

Rates rise. The price she would get if she sold today falls to $800. The coupon is still $40.

steps.prompt: If Helen sells today at $800, how many dollars does she get?
steps.explain: The sale price is $800. That is $200 below the $1,000 face value.

steps.prompt: If she holds and the issuer pays at maturity, how many dollars of face value come back?
steps.explain: Maturity pays the $1,000 face value. The $800 was the “sell today” price, not the end.

steps.prompt: Helen’s coupon changed to $32 because the price fell.
steps.explain: The coupon stays $40. The price fell so a new buyer’s yield can compete.

steps.prompt: What is Helen’s fitting move if she still does not need the money?
choices: Hold to maturity, since that was the plan
Borrow to buy more of the same bond
steps.explain: The plan was 10 years. The screen price is for someone who sells today.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Bonds & Interest Rates
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A bond pays a $50 coupon and you buy it for $1,000. What is the yield, in percent?
You can redeem a new I bond in the first 12 months.
steps.explain: The first year is locked. Before five years, cashing out also costs the last three months of interest.

steps.prompt: Rates rise and you sell a bond before maturity. What is the usual price effect?
choices: The price is frozen at face value
steps.explain: Existing bonds get cheaper so their yield can compete with new, higher rates.

steps.prompt: What is the electronic I bond cap, in dollars, for one person in a calendar year?
steps.explain: The cap is $10,000. This trial asks the cap, not today’s changing rate.
